items.title: We’re launching VIALS-AA, a leaderboard for Handshake AI’s VIALS benchmark for visual reasoning in l...
items.content:
We’re launching VIALS-AA, a leaderboard for Handshake AI’s VIALS benchmark for visual reasoning in life sciences and biotech research

Visual artifacts are central to how scientists analyze experiments and make research decisions, but interpreting them correctly remains a challenge for frontier models. VIALS’ 161 tasks span eight domains and need models to reason over artifacts including gel blots, flow cytometry plots, plasmid maps, and phylogenies. Each task requires models to interpret an artifact and draw a specific scientific conclusion.

We evaluate models by running each task three times in Stirrup, our open source agent harness, with code execution and image inspection tools. GPT-6 Luna (medium) grades each answer against the reference answer, and we report the share of tasks judged correct in all three repeats (pass^3).

Key takeaways:

➤ The top three models are separated by 3 points: Gemini 4 Carbon (high) from @GoogleDeepMind leads narrowly with 64%, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 63% and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) from @AnthropicAI at 61%

➤ Astra and Sol achieve similar scores to Opus and Sonnet at a much lower Cost per Task: Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) averages $1.64 per task, ~29× as much as Sol (~$0.056). This price difference is significantly driven by turn use - GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) average ~8 turns per task, compared with ~27 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) and ~25 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback)

➤ Open weights models trail the highest score by ~19 points: Kimi K3.1 Pro leads open weights models on VIALS-AA at 45%, narrowly ahead of MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 43%

➤ 14 of 161 tasks saw safety refusals on at least one model: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) refused on 6 tasks, the most of any model, and half of the 14 affected tasks saw refusals from multiple models

Thank you to @joinHandshakeAI and the VIALS authors for creating the benchmark and collaborating with us on bringing it to Artificial Analysis!

items.title: Open-source is critical for robotics AI. It means a student, a researcher or a startup can build on ...
items.content:
Open-source is critical for robotics AI. It means a student, a researcher or a startup can build on years of progress and contribute something the whole community can use rather than concentrating everything in a few companies building a black-box robot. 

That’s why we’re building @huggingface into the platform for open-source robotics AI! Amazing to see the progress we've made in the six months and it's accelerating!

- Almost 100,000 public robotics datasets on https://t.co/QIPmkxCk57, up 48%
- Over 30,000 public robotics models, up 41%
- Microduck and Reachy mini, our open-source robots became the most popular robot of 2026 (probably ending the year with 50,000+ sold and 20,000+ shipped)
- We’re a founding partner of @RoboColosseum, evaluating robots across 140+ real-world scenes. Every run is published publicly on HF, including failures, so everyone can learn from what actually happens.

And @LeRobotHF got downloaded over 1M times and v0.7.0 just landed with new world action models, interactive robot control and remote GPU inference: https://t.co/Euoz11Ccc5!

Huge thanks to everyone making this happen 🤗🦾

D...
items.content:
A new way to measure how AI agents handle the routine analyses of wet-lab science—BioBasicsBench.

Developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, the benchmark draws on 100 tasks from real experiments to test whether agents can interpret raw lab data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence doesn’t support a conclusion.

Accelerating biological research starts with getting the everyday work right. BioBasicsBench shows where models need to improve, and helps us track what those gains mean for scientific progress, biosafety, and biosecurity.

https://t.co/wN2xLk0YeW

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash speeds on GB300 NVL72 have increased by up to 1.5x tok/s per agent over the past...
items.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash speeds on GB300 NVL72 have increased by up to 1.5x tok/s per agent over the past month on AA-AgentPerf, our benchmark of datacenter systems running realistic agentic coding workloads

This improvement comes from a newer vLLM version, new vLLM kernels for DeepSeek V4.1 on GB300, FlashInfer autotuning, fuller CUDA graph coverage, tuned speculative decoding, and running prefill and decode on the same GPUs in NVIDIA’s updated Dynamo + vLLM setup

➤ Faster speeds: 848 tok/s for a single agent, up from 596 (1.42x)

➤ Higher throughput: ~1.6x the throughput per GPU at ~80 tok/s per agent

items.title: If you pretrain a large enough transformer on text files with the LLM weights (which are in abundanc...
items.content:
If you pretrain a large enough transformer on text files with the LLM weights (which are in abundance on Hugging Face and GitHub), it will learn to understand the meaning of and connection between the weights the same way it learned to understand the meaning of and the connection between words and elements of programming code.

If you then finetune this model on examples of editing such files, it will learn to edit these weights.

Transformer doesn't care about what's in a text file: Shakespeare, Linux, or Qwen. As long as there are tokens, it will learn to predict the next one.

Transformer doesn't care about what's in a text file: Shakespeare, Linux, or Qwen. As long as there are tokens, it will learn to predict the next one.

items.content:
Five predictions about what might come next:

1. AI isn’t not over. [Did anyone actually say “AI is over” after the DeepSeek moment? (I did not. Is anyone saying that now? I am not.]

2. What might actually be over is the era of insanely high valuations - for generative AI — and exponentially increasing investments in data centers.

3. People will continue to use generative AI (now mostly via harnessed neurosymbolic models with tools and loops rather than the once dominant pure LLMs that are no longer popular).

4. New, more reliable architectures will eventually displace today’s AI, but it may take several years, or more.

5. A newer generation of AI will actually be worth a lot of money; this one was overrated and people will eventually see that in hindsight.

cc @dee_bosa

Scientific models help ...
items.content:
New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

items.title: OpenAI's GPT Image 2.6 takes #1 and #2 on both AA-Image-T2I v2.1 and AA-Image-Editing v2.1. GPT Imag...
items.content:
OpenAI's GPT Image 2.6 takes #1 and #2 on both AA-Image-T2I v2.1 and AA-Image-Editing v2.1. GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare with slightly better quality, and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst takes the top spot with longer generation times

OpenAI released GPT Image 2.6 on November 4 in ChatGPT, Codex and the API. The API offers two models, GPT Image 2.6 Flare and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst, which follow GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst. Both support Text to Image and Image Editing, and add animated GIF and SVG output. OpenAI added a complexity setting to the API, which controls how much the model plans before rendering. We benchmarked both models at max quality, with complexity at its API default of high.

In our testing, GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare while delivering slightly better quality. Its median Text to Image generation time fell from about 55 to 30 seconds, and its editing time fell from about 58 to 32 seconds. GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst goes the other way: it takes longer than GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, at about 2 minutes 15 seconds per image, and takes the #1 spot. Its largest Text to Image gains are in Reasoning, Text Rendering, Lighting and Material, and it is strongest in UIUX Design.

Both models cost $30 per 1M image output tokens, the same as GPT Image 2.5. That is about $0.21 per 1024x1024 image at max quality ($211 per 1k images).

GPT Image 2.6 is available in ChatGPT and Codex across all tiers, and in the OpenAI API.

Congratulations to @OpenAI on the release!

See below for our analysis of GPT Image 2.6 in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title:
Similar VIALS-AA scores can result from very different approaches to visual reasoning

Claude Opus 5...
items.content:
Similar VIALS-AA scores can result from very different approaches to visual reasoning

Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) averages ~32 tool calls per task, compared with ~8 for GPT-6 Astra, while their VIALS-AA scores are similar (61% and 63%, respectively). This is because Opus performs extensive annotation and measurement, averaging ~8 Image Measurement tool calls per task, compared to ~0.4 for Astra. Image Viewing accounts for a larger share of Astra’s tool calls at ~51% vs. ~42% for Opus

items.title:
Personal news: I’m joining Sound Ventures as an advisor.

Fun story, Guy Oseary first reached out ba...
items.content:
Personal news: I’m joining Sound Ventures as an advisor.

Fun story, Guy Oseary first reached out back when The Rundown had 150K subscribers.

I had no idea what I was doing, and I’m still not sure why he took the call...

But we’re at 3.5M now, and I’ve learned he has a real gift for spotting talent early, whether that’s in music or through early investments like OpenAI and Anthropic. 

Fortunate to be on the receiving end of that, and even more grateful for his mentorship along the way!

What makes Sound different is how much they focus on brand, marketing, storytelling, and distribution, which in my opinion is the most important thing right now.

It’s never been easier or cheaper to start a company, but the flip side is that new startups pop up in the same categories every day. What makes one stand out is the ability to tell its story.

I’ll also be getting a closer look at what’s coming before it’s obvious, and I’ll be sharing what I’m seeing with you.

Excited to join my friends Roberto (@rpn) and Tiff (@TiffinTech_ ) as advisors alongside a deep bench of marketing and media minds.

Let’s go.

items.title: How online services will die. I already posted recently about how I imported my liked songs from Spo...
items.content:
How online services will die. I already posted recently about how I imported my liked songs from Spotify into YouTube Music by asking Codex to do it. There are several popular online services that do this, but now they're irrelevant.

Here's one more example. To save time, when I built ChapterPal, I used a dedicated online service with a generous free allowance to resize and cache images.

At some point (many months later), the number of image resize requests exceeded the free allowance. The service sent me an email saying that it would stop serving my requests if I didn't switch to its paid plan.

What I did was ask Codex what was included in my plan with Cloudflare, and it said that image resizing and caching were included.

So, I asked Codex to rewrite the code to use Cloudflare.

Then Cloudflare started sending me invoices for the resizing calls, but not for the caching.

So, I asked Codex to implement the resizing on the backend and use Cloudflare only the caching.

I also developed ChapterPal to use the Cloud Run feature on GCP when longer processing is needed than a Supabase edge function can support.

In the beginning, ChapterPal didn't generate many calls to these Cloud Run containers, but over time, GCP started sending me serious invoices because Cloud Run is billed per second.

So, I asked Codex to rent a VPS outside GCP and move the container execution environment there instead of using GCP.

Now, GCP only sends me invoices for the container registry, so I'm thinking about asking Codex to build a local container registry in Supabase storage.

Eventually, I will move everything to a service provider that provides the thinnest layer of infrastructure on top of bare metal for the lowest price, so Supabase and VPS providers won't be needed either.
items.author: @burkov
items.summary: Andriy Burkov argues that many niche online services will die because coding agents make them replaceable: he used Codex to migrate Spotify playlists, then to replace an image-resizing/caching service with Cloudflare, and then to move resizing in-house when Cloudflare billed for it, eliminating the need for the third-party tool.
items.reasoning: Original, concrete first-person illustration of how agentic coding erodes the SaaS long tail; decent engagement (3.5K views) and a genuinely interesting thesis from a known ML author.

items.title:
The model claims that committed text never changes.

It learns this with Longest Stable Prefix (LSP)...
items.content:
The model claims that committed text never changes.

It learns this with Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) supervision: train on the longest stable prefix given the available audio, and emit WAIT when the continuation is uncertain.

Training combines SFT with GRPO reinforcement learning. The paper proves that the prefix never shrinks, matches the full-audio output, and stays as long as possible while remaining stable.

This works with vLLM/Transformers.

items.title: Axios cofounder @roylschwartz says Fortune 500 executives are worried AI is creating more work for e...
items.content:
Axios cofounder @roylschwartz says Fortune 500 executives are worried AI is creating more work for employees instead of making them more productive:

"Work slop, right? The problem is everyone now has access to AI. They're writing longer emails."

"They're writing more reports. They're doing more presentations, and then they're sending it out to all of their colleagues."

"Everyone feels like, 'Oh, I'm gonna sound great. I'm gonna sound super smart, and I'm gonna use AI to make my point.' And so everything just gets longer, and unfortunately, in the short term at least, more complicated."

"We've talked to CEOs, executives at Fortune 500 companies, and their biggest worry right now is AI slop and it creating more work for their employees."

"A report that gets generated using AI that might be twice as long as it needs to be."

"Information now has to be presented in a way that's far more efficient than ever before."
@axios

Axios cofounder @roylschwartz says Fortune 500 executives are worried AI is creating more work for employees instead of making them more productive:

"Work slop, right? The problem is everyone now has access to AI. They're writing longer emails."

"They're writing more reports. They're doing more presentations, and then they're sending it out to all of their colleagues."

"Everyone feels like, 'Oh, I'm gonna sound great. I'm gonna sound super smart, and I'm gonna use AI to make my point.' And so everything just gets longer, and unfortunately, in the short term at least, more complicated."

"We've talked to CEOs, executives at Fortune 500 companies, and their biggest worry right now is AI slop and it creating more work for their employees."

"A report that gets generated using AI that might be twice as long as it needs to be."

"Information now has to be presented in a way that's far more efficient than ever before."

@axios

• The encoder produces one audio token every 80ms...
items.content:
Here is how the streaming inference engine works:

• The encoder produces one audio token every 80ms.
• The decoder processes chunks at 160ms per chunk.

That means 6.25 updates per second.

Keeping the real-time factor below 1 requires each update to finish before the next chunk arrives.

Here is what they do:

1. KV cache management with W=1 retained window: cache completed windows and re-prefill the active window.

2. Speculative decoding: reuse the previous suffix as a draft, verify it, and decode only disagreements.

3. Chunk-wise decoding with optimized prefill.

items.title: @martin_casado cool to see we're landing on a similar approach to safe self-modification! https://t....
items.content:
@martin_casado cool to see we're landing on a similar approach to safe self-modification! https://t.co/gMouW0sTCS

via @grok:

"Both treat the harness/runtime as the place to improve (not weights), and both lean hard on a durable substrate so self-modification doesn’t destroy the agent. Exo and Regimes both preserve an append-only history/log that survives rewinds or restarts, so the system can inspect what actually happened and recover. Both make changes inspectable and try to keep the “mechanism” (state, recovery, activation control) protected while letting policy evolve. In short: systems thinking over pure prompt engineering.

Differences

Exo collapses the optimization loop into the live task. The agent can look at its own code and runtime logs mid-work and freely edit the evolvable policy layer (prompts, context assembly, tools, even how it improves itself), then the guardian rebuilds and can roll back. It’s broader, more free-form code-level self-editing, optimized for efficiency gains while the work is still running.

Regimes is a more controlled, offline-style improvement loop on top of ActiveGraph. It diagnoses failure regimes, routes them to specific typed pipeline seams, has the model propose a scoped repair (often a prompt or transform), and only promotes it after static checks + sandbox + in-sample + held-out validation. Everything is event-sourced so the whole loop is replayable and auditable. It’s narrower, more gated, and prioritizes trustworthy accuracy improvements over open-ended runtime rewriting.

Exo is “let the agent rewrite itself safely while it works.” Regimes is “diagnose the failure mode, patch only the right seam, and only keep it if it generalizes.”

Ruby Justice-Thelot argues AI has put Bell Labs in every creative's bedroom, giving artists access to tools that once required the resources of a major research lab:

"There was a steady sort of interest in the field, but it really jumped in 2025. And I think in part this is due to the unlock of creativity led by artificial intelligence."

"If people had ideas for novel interfaces, novel things to do with the computer, their limitation was in part due to their technical ability."

"Armed with the latest large language models, they find themselves in Bell Labs, in Xerox PARC, working with EAT, but in the comfort of their own bedrooms."

"What once required the buy-in from a large corporation to give you access to compute, I think now is made much easier by the broadening of accessibility that is led by AI."

Ruby Justice-Thelot explains why creatives are losing their technical moat when AI can recreate a viral visual effect from just a screenshot in days:

Sofia: "Everyone else is shooting their own videos, doing some edit, and then posting them, and that's just what music marketing has started to become."

"The feedback loop for when you make something versus when everyone sees it and then everyone starts to copy it is so fast. I see trends get fulfilled within like 3 days."

Ruby: "If I can take a screenshot of the video, I can see the echo effect that they put on TouchDesigner, describe it, and then be able to recreate that by the end of the week, if not even faster."

"The moat here for these creatives is in part how rapid they are in executing their creative visions. I don't think it's a technical moat anymore."

Traversal CEO @_anish_agarwal reveals AI coding agents are creating a new problem for enterprises:

More code, more complexity, and increasingly difficult software failures that nobody knows how to fix.

"When an incident happens, you don't know it's a security threat. Is it someone internally broke it? And you'll have thousands of people in a war room trying to figure out why it broke."

"That's becoming even worse now with all the coding agents because they’re just writing so much more code, they're doing so much more complex workloads, and no one really understands the code they’re writing."

"It's becoming top of mind for CIOs and CTOs of, 'How do I maintain all the software in production and keep it reliable and safe?'"

items.content:
One of my biggest motivations to make web games (the original motivation for my fly-pieter-com game) or port existing games to the web is how incredibly slow the loading times of modern games have become

I have an RTX 5090 w/ 32GB GDDR7 liquid cooled maxed out gaming PC with 128GB DDR5 RAM, a 16-core 32-thread AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D and a Corsair 4TB NVMe SSD

And it still takes almost 3 minutes just to load Flight Simulator, and that's after loading it a few minutes before already to install the updates

You can call me impatient, but you used to just put you'd run a game and you'd start playing within 30 seconds or instantly!

That's how it should be I think!

items.title: GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare on both Text to Image and Image E...
items.content:
GPT Image 2.6 Flare is almost twice as fast as GPT Image 2.5 Flare on both Text to Image and Image Editing, while GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst takes longer than GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst

In our Text to Image speed benchmark, Flare's median generation time fell from about 55 seconds to about 30 seconds. In our Image Editing timing run, it fell from about 58 seconds to about 32 seconds. Flare is now level with GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst's quality on AA-Image-T2I v2.1 in about a quarter of the time. On our Quality vs Speed chart, Flare is the only model in the most attractive quadrant.

Sunburst takes about 2 minutes 15 seconds per Text to Image generation and about 2 minutes per edit, longer than GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst in every run we paired. The extra time comes with the #1 spot on AA-Image-T2I v2.1.

➤ Median generation time: 1024x1024 PNG at max quality, on the OpenAI API

items.content:
Streaming gains extend to 18 test sets across 10 additional languages, all improving over the base model.

Four areas I'd like to see more tests:

1. Self-consistent LSP: derive targets from the streaming model's own outputs to potentially move beyond the base model's ceiling.

2. Adaptive chunks: vary chunk size with audio complexity to improve the latency–accuracy trade-off.

3. Continuous rewards: add confidence estimates to improve calibration and streaming decisions.

4. Encoder adapters: test lightweight LoRA adapters for specialized domains.

I shut down my 13-year old $300/mo Linode VPS server that hosted al...
items.content:
I did the same a few months ago

I shut down my 13-year old $300/mo Linode VPS server that hosted all my 100+ sites for over a decade!

That Linode VPS called Tommy is where everything started for me, I knew to build startups I needed a server so I just made one and SSH'd into it and started uploading PHP files of little startups I made

After 1.5 years my first sites started taking off and I started making money on the internet with Tommy!

For almost a decade I'd still FTP my files by dragging them every time I made an edit to the server, only around 2020 I switched to Github because @daniellockyer said it'd be better and because regularly the site would break at halfway because people would load the site while I was in the middle transferring index.php over FTP 😂

I didn't have multiple VPS servers, I had just one for ALL my sites and projects (I'd say upwards of 100), but it worked mostly fine, and I regularly posted about how it was all on one server which made Twitter/X go crazy "how do you scale???", it scaled fine, served 300 million people per year and 115,000 paying customers in its lifetime!

Back around 2013, Linode was the "cool" hoster on Hacker News, but a decade later, the spirit of Linode seemed to have disappeared, it felt like it was in maintenance mode and not really loved for anymore. When it was acquired by Akamai in 2022, me and @daniellockyer knew we'd have to leave because acquired companies generally go to shit

I saw @DHH posting about @Hetzner_Online so I started making little VPS servers there to test it, first with @pieter and it worked really great. Then slowly I started migrating each site over to Hetzner, with the most critical sites like Photo AI and Nomads last. I also started separating sites on to different VPS servers, isolating them, which now in this new AI cybersecurity time makes security sense. It was never an issue with performance though to have 100+ sites on one VPS, like literally never at all

Then a few months ago I had to finally press the button to switch Tommy off, forever, I mean how nerd is it is to have feelings about a VPS? But without this little server I wouldn't have my life right now. 

I always imagined Tommy as some 🐻 brown bear, so I made it a little retirement page where it's sipping coconuts and chilling on the beach 🙏😊 THANK YOU TOMMY!!!!

🐻 https://t.co/vbvfcvR9y6

items.content:
Victorians tried to communicate with the dead through the telegraph. Today, TikTok's "This message is for you" videos make people feel personally chosen by the algorithm.

Ruby Justice-Thelot explains why we keep giving new technology supernatural powers:

"If it started with, 'This message is for you,' it meant that you had been selected by the algorithm to receive this blessing."

"My own sort of turn of phrase on this is that with every new technology, we find new ways of believing."

"The spiritualists, upon the invention of the telegraph, sought to use it to speak to the netherworlds."

"Our impulse to ascribe these supernatural capabilities are still the same that we had in Victorian England with radio, with TV. It is now just with the algorithm."

items.title: The 300M-parameter audio encoder and projector stay frozen throughout post-training on about 1,500 h...
items.content:
The 300M-parameter audio encoder and projector stay frozen throughout post-training on about 1,500 hours of audio.

Training has two stages:

1. SFT on LSP transcription and WAIT targets.

2. GRPO with accuracy and precision rewards, plus length and repetition penalties, to reduce hallucinations, repetition, and language inconsistency.

Freezing the encoder preserves its pretrained acoustic representations but limits domain adaptation.

Now hundreds of open-weight mode...
items.content:
"AGI was achieved in February 2026 when Claude Opus 4.6 launched."

Now hundreds of open-weight models running locally can outperform it, says StackAI cofounder @BernAceituno:

"Last year has been really the advent of open source. Past few weeks we've seen a Cambrian explosion of open source models."

"I always say, and I stand by this, that AGI was achieved in February 2026 around the time Opus 4.6 came to the market."

"Today there's hundreds of open-weight models that perform better than this closed-form model, just running in a local computer, and that's mind-blowing."

"The frontier will always set the pace and the open-weight model will lag behind. But the open-weight community will catch up. At one point you start realizing, okay, what’s my trade-off on investment, governance, and residency?"
@stackai @asana

items.title:
The U parameter lets you adjust quality versus latency without retraining:

• U=1 prioritizes qualit...
items.content:
The U parameter lets you adjust quality versus latency without retraining:

• U=1 prioritizes quality
• U=0 prioritizes latency

The reported combined macro-average error is 5.76% across 13 test sets.

At 160ms chunks, withholding one token reduces macro-average error by about 10%.

➤ Object-Level Edit: adding, removing, replacing or altering specific objects in the frame.

➤ Identity Preserving Edit: changing people, faces or characters while keeping their identity intact.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit: working out what to change from the scene, rather than following a literal instruction.

➤ Scene & Style Edit: relighting or restyling the image, or changing its background, setting or overall look.

items.title: Introduction to Scientific Programming with Python by Joakim Sundnes is now in the @ChapterPal's col...
items.content:
Introduction to Scientific Programming with Python by Joakim Sundnes is now in the @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

Python is a free, high-level, general-purpose programming language designed to be easy for humans to read and write. Created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991, its syntax closely resembles spoken English, which reduces the complexity of writing software and makes it the world's most popular language for beginners and professionals alike.

Unlike low-level languages that require complex instructions to talk to computer hardware, Python acts as a bridge, utilizing a separate program called an interpreter to translate clean, simple text commands into machine code that the computer can execute on the fly.

Python is a de-facto standard programming language for AI, machine learning, and data science.

items.title:
iOS 27 has broken the amazingly useful Low Light feature (inside Zoom) combined with Smart Invert

I...
items.content:
iOS 27 has broken the amazingly useful Low Light feature (inside Zoom) combined with Smart Invert

If anyone works at @Apple, or knows anyone there, it'd be amazing to get this working again!

Bug report and prompt for Apple staff to copy paste into their clanker to fix it:

"## Bug: Zoom "Low Light" filter + Smart Invert makes the screen brighter instead of darker (regression in iOS 27)

### Summary
Before iOS 27, turning on Smart Invert together with the Zoom filter "Low Light" made the screen very dark. Many users rely on this to read at night, like a Kindle. In iOS 27 the same combination makes the screen noticeably BRIGHTER than Smart Invert alone: the background looks washed-out light grey and the text is full white.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size → turn on Smart Invert.
2. Settings → Accessibility → Zoom → turn on Zoom, set Zoom Filter to "Low Light", Zoom Region to Full Screen, and zoom level 1.0x (or the lowest possible).
3. Open a white page, e.g. Safari or Books.
4. Compare the screen with Low Light on and off.

### Expected (iOS 26 and earlier)
- White background → near black
- Black text → dim grey
- Result: darker than Smart Invert alone

### Actual (iOS 27)
- White background → light grey (~70%)
- Black text → full white
- Result: brighter and lower contrast than Smart Invert alone

### Likely root cause
The order of the two filters seems to have been swapped in the display/compositing pipeline.

- Old order: Smart Invert → Low Light (invert, then dim)
  - Output = 0.3 × (1 − x), which is always dark
- New order: Low Light → Smart Invert (dim, then invert)
  - Output = 1 − 0.3 × x, which is mostly bright, because inverting a dimmed image turns the dimming into brightening

The washed-out grey look is the typical sign of dimming before inverting. My guess is that a refactor in iOS 27 moved Smart Invert into a final full-screen pass, or moved the Zoom filter earlier in the chain, so Low Light now runs underneath the inversion instead of on top of it.

### Task
1. Find where the Zoom filters (Low Light, Grayscale, Inverted, etc.) and Smart Invert / Classic Invert are applied in the render/compositor pipeline. Compare this ordering between iOS 26 and iOS 27 to find the change that swapped them.
2. Restore the old behavior: Low Light (and any other dimming/brightness-reducing Zoom filter) must be applied AFTER Smart Invert and Classic Invert.
3. Keep the iOS 27 change that caused this if it fixed something else (e.g. correct inversion of new UI materials). Fix only the ordering of the Zoom filter relative to the invert pass, not the whole refactor.
4. Check that other combinations still work as before:
   - Low Light + Classic Invert
   - Low Light + Reduce White Point
   - Low Light + Dark Mode
   - Grayscale Zoom filter + Smart Invert
   - Color Filters + Smart Invert
   - Zoom at 1.0x and higher magnification, Full Screen and Window zoom
   - Screenshots and screen recordings (check what is captured matches expectations)
5. Add a regression test that renders a white frame with Smart Invert + Low Light enabled. It should assert the output brightness is LOWER than with Smart Invert alone.

### Acceptance criteria
- Smart Invert + Low Light gives a darker screen than Smart Invert alone, matching iOS 26 behavior.
- No change to the other accessibility filter combinations listed above.
- The regression test passes and is in CI.

### Why it matters
This is a popular accessibility workaround for light sensitivity and night reading. Many low-vision and light-sensitive users depend on it, and Apple has no other built-in way to get the screen this dark."

THANK YOU!

items.title:
G-NLL 

Natural Language Generation (NLG) represents a revolutionary frontier in artificial intellig...
items.content:
G-NLL 

Natural Language Generation (NLG) represents a revolutionary frontier in artificial intelligence, empowering machines to produce text that mirrors human expression. By harnessing the latest developments in deep learning, researchers are crafting systems that generate responses that are not only contextually relevant but also remarkably coherent. The potential applications are vast and impactful, ranging from streamlined customer support to inspiring creative writing and enabling real-time translation. This technology highlights the power of seamless communication between humans and machines, paving the way for enhanced interaction in our increasingly digital world.

A significant challenge in the realm of Natural Language Generation is evaluating the reliability of machine-generated text. Given their probabilistic design, language models can yield different outputs for identical input prompts, introducing variability that can undermine the trustworthiness of the content produced. This inconsistency raises essential questions about the model’s confidence in its predictions. Tackling this challenge is vital, especially in high-stakes applications like medical or legal documentation, where precision and dependability are crucial. Ensuring the accuracy of these outputs is essential for fostering user trust and achieving effective communication in critical fields.

To gauge uncertainty in machine generated text, conventional methods often involve sampling multiple output sequences and assessing them as a whole. While these approaches can provide valuable insights, they require considerable computational resources, as generating numerous sequences is inherently resource-intensive. As a result, the feasibility of implementing these methods diminishes for larger-scale applications or when dealing with complex language models. This limitation underscores the need for more efficient strategies that can accurately estimate uncertainty without imposing heavy computational demands.

Researchers from the ELLIS Unit Linz and LIT AI Lab at Johannes Kepler University Linz, Austria, have unveiled an innovative method known as, G-NLL, to enhance the process of estimation. This approach revolves around calculating the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the most probable output sequence. Unlike previous methods that depend on sampling multiple sequences, G-NLL employs decoding to pinpoint the most likely sequence and assess its likelihood efficiently. By concentrating on this single sequence, the method significantly improves the efficiency of computational demands, presenting a more streamlined and effective estimation in language models.

This inconsistency raises essential questions about the model’s confidence in its predictions. Tackling this challenge is vital, especially in high-stakes applications like medical or legal documentation, where precision and dependability are crucial. Ensuring the accuracy of these outputs is essential for fostering user trust and achieving effective communication in critical fields.

To gauge uncertainty in machine generated text, conventional methods often involve sampling multiple output sequences and assessing them as a whole. While these approaches can provide valuable insights, they require considerable computational resources, as generating numerous sequences is inherently resource-intensive. As a result, the feasibility of implementing these methods diminishes for larger-scale applications or when dealing with complex language models. This limitation underscores the need for more efficient strategies that can accurately estimate uncertainty without imposing heavy computational demands.

Researchers from the ELLIS Unit Linz and LIT AI Lab at Johannes Kepler University Linz, Austria, have unveiled an innovative method known as, G-NLL, to enhance the process of estimation. This approach revolves around calculating the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the most probable output sequence. Unlike previous methods that depend on sampling multiple sequences, G-NLL employs decoding to pinpoint the most likely sequence and assess its likelihood efficiently. By concentrating on this single sequence, the method significantly improves the efficiency of computational demands, presenting a more streamlined and effective estimation in language models.
